doc.title: Ada Rovatti interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 13, 2022

title: Soloing over one chord and playing out
summary: She contrasts vamps with changes and describes playing dissonant against a chord to open the ears.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Do you find that, I won’t say easier — how is it different if you’re soloing over a vamp on one chord rather than playing changes like on a hard bop tune? Is your thought process different?

Well you know it’s just with one chord of course it also depends also on the band you are playing with, it’s just like a blank, it’s a white canvas that you can just go in the direction you want. With one chord and then just like play out, in and out, and just kind of rhythmically — you study, there is a specific form with a specific rhythm and the chords change clearly you have some flexibility of reharmonization and playing in and out but you still have to kind of follow the chords and the form. So it’s a different kind of approach. But it’s just like, you know, sometimes — one exercise I like to do just to open my ears, you know a lot of people say when you play out what do you think — it’s just

like I think it comes down to confidence and just bend the boundaries that we have in our inner ears. You know if you’re playing in C, and sometimes I put one of those Aebersold like C7 and the band plays C7. And I keep playing B7 or C#7 or F#7 and these totally out you know, clashing. But if you keep playing against those chords, you’re going to realize that your brain little by little easing up, It doesn’t hear that much, that dissonance. And as a matter of fact when you go back, in C, it sounds as if you’re messing it up. Your brain kind of like suddenly is like what are you playing? And I’m playing C over C. But just that tells you that it’s all here, the dissonance. And it’s fun to just play in a totally dissonant and go in and out of the chords, it’s just the way also to pulling the audience, it’s like look at me now, look what I do. And they kind of don’t get it but then they feel relaxed when you go back in the key. So it’s just a way of teasing your ears, the musician, it’s just a game you know.
Oh that’s wonderful. No one ever said that exactly like that.
It’s a way of teasing your senses, let’s put it like that.
